statements.text:
https://t.co/YzfQS59s91's successful release of GLM-5.2 underscores China's growing challenge to America's lead in AI – not merely by narrowing the gap on models’ power, but because of the open-source, compute-efficient nature of Chinese models.

The growing cybersecurity and national security risks posed by these Chinese models reinforce why the U.S.  cannot afford opaque Commerce Dept decisions, lacking any transparent standards, that limit the public’s access to frontier AI models.

Shutting down frontier AI models too rashly makes U.S. institutions–including hospitals, local governments, utilities, and financial institutions–much more vulnerable to cybersecurity risk. We are in a race against time: we must enable Americans to deploy the most powerful AI models to identify and patch cyber vulnerabilities in critical systems before malevolent actors can use AI tools to exploit them.

If the Trump Administration wants to play gatekeeper with the world’s most consequential technology, Americans deserve clear, objective, principled criteria that distinguish between acceptable and unacceptable risks.

The Department of Commerce reversed its decision to restrict Anthropic’s frontier AI models, but we still don’t know why. 

The Administration’s standards, criteria, and evidentiary thresholds remain murky. 

The public and developers deserve transparent, objective rules applied consistently to regulate humanity’s most consequential technology.

Taking the lead of the Chinese Communist Party, President Donald Trump has the government take equity stakes in more than a dozen corporations, and wants to take shares in AI companies. For many reasons, this is a bad idea; we need the government to regulate industry objectively, and when necessary, to protect the public from bad actors–not to take a cut of the profits when people cut corners. We can ensure that Americans benefit from AI by regulating AI sensibly, and by fixing our broken tax system.

We rarely hear elected leaders discuss solutions with any depth or nuance. Even less frequently do we engage in public conversations about those ideas.   

Doing so requires that we get beyond the infantilizing tone of political discourse on social media and TV, and we treat each other like adults. 

So, I'm joining Substack. And I’d like to recruit you.

I’m recruiting a corps of solution-oriented Americans committed to governance by, and for, grownups. This space is for those who want to engage seriously about solving our nation's biggest problems. I welcome your feedback and better ideas.  

We’ll have a conversation–about AI, housing affordability, and jobs of the future–like adults.

We can’t know what skills workers will need a decade from now, but we can be certain that our private sector employers will know before we do. The SKILL Act moves us beyond the failed federal job retraining programs of the past to engage companies in investing in our community colleges and state universities to build training programs that will actually get  Americans better jobs—and an economic future— in an AI-driven economy.

The Trump Administration wants to be the final arbiter of the truth, controlling what frontier AI models tell you. The FTC has proposed a policy to penalize AI companies whose output has any "undisclosed ideology.”  How does a Trump-controlled FTC regulate an AI LLM for providing the truth about January 6th, or the results of the 2020 election? No President–and certainly not this one–should play truth-verifier-in-chief. We have less than one month to let the Administration know that we won't stand for this: go to https://t.co/Dqi7DbHbtj to learn more.

Rather than flailing at any attempts to enforce a “ban” on open weight Chinese AI models, the Trump Administration would do better to identify and broadcast the lack of security and potential backdoors of Kimi 3, GLM, DeepSeek and others — the liability risks will dissuade many corporate users from doing so. We win when we compete better.

If top frontier AI model developers cannot anticipate jailbreaks and control agentic misalignment, we cannot expect government regulators will. We need a regulatory approach that massively re-aligns developer incentives toward AI safety and security, as I’ve publicly proposed below.

Hyperscalers have plenty of capital to do AI research;  they don’t need the taxpayers’ money, too.

Federal research dollars must remain focused on the kind of basic research that the private sector won’t fund, because it remains too distant from commercial application. That approach has worked pretty well in the U.S. since the days of Vannevar Bush in the 1940’s.

After such a consequential week for AI, with the leading labs demonstrating real progress, today's news feels especially timely: @SVAngel is launching Project Blueprint, a comprehensive effort to forge consensus among industry leaders and lawmakers around durable solutions to the hardest AI policy challenges so that all Americans can benefit from AI's opportunities. We are encouraged by the reaction of Sam Altman, Dario Amodei and Demis Hassabis to the launch of Project Blueprint:

Sam Altman, co-founder and CEO of OpenAI: "We have before us a technology of immense and still-unfolding wonder. I believe AI has the power to heal people, to discover cures and to deliver abundance on a scale the world has never known before. But we need a way for the world to build trust in the technology so that we can all get to share these benefits. National safety requirements for the most capable systems are a great first step, ideally building towards a global framework for advanced AI models. I’m glad Ron is bringing the people building AI and policymakers together to help move that work forward.”

Dario Amodei, CEO and co-founder, Anthropic: "AI is advancing faster than our institutions can adapt, and the most important decisions about how it is developed and deployed will be made in the next few years. If those decisions are to serve the public, they can't rest with AI companies alone. Industry and policymakers need to work through them together, with an honest, shared understanding of what these systems can do. We're glad to support Project Blueprint's effort to make that possible." 

Demis Hassabis, chairman and co-founder of Google DeepMind and the chief scientist of Alphabet: "We have long said that AI development needs to be both bold and responsible. We support bringing industry and lawmakers together around public policies that promote both innovation and safety."

statements.quoted: Democrats are trying to dismiss the White House Accord on Super Intelligence as optional self-policing. But although the agreement was entered into voluntarily, the governance that follows from it is not. As Gavin Baker points out, once an independent auditor reports a safety issue to an independent board committee, directors have a fiduciary duty not to disregard it, and a D&O carrier can use a bad-faith finding to deny coverage. So although the agreement starts with internal controls, these are verified by external audit and board oversight — and then existing FTC and securities law still apply to any public claim the company does not keep. This is far more practical than what Democrats want — a freeze on frontier development while China races ahead. Democrats should applaud what President Trump has accomplished. But they would rather use SI safety as a campaign issue than admit the Accord represents major progress.

statements.quoted:
interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

SCOOP: Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents inside customer accounts, including some attempting to take actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, sources told Axios.

The findings have alarmed banking executives, who are racing to restrict access to their systems as AI moves at a velocity faster than financial institutions can respond, multiple industry and bank executives told Axios.

Several banks are now preparing for worst-case and even “day after” scenarios, including how to rapidly secure or restore customer accounts if things go wrong, the people said.

Several bank executives told Axios they're struggling to distinguish between human users and AI agents. One executive said banks also struggle to determine whether agents are authorized by customers or potentially operating without their permission, more akin to rogue agent behavior.

Despite staggering advances in basic science, drug development research is only getting slower. The main culprit? Increasing clinical trial timelines. The median clinical development pathway has increased from 8.4 years to 9.3 years and pipeline creation has slowed 32% even as R&D spend has gone up. 

This is the point I keep making about the main bottleneck to drug discovery and why AI on its own won't be enough. These timelines aren't going anywhere (ofc AI can be used creatively to ease such bottlenecks -- eg via better endpoints that allow smaller cohorts for trials, followed up for shorter periods of time).
